title: Metamemory and Confidence
content_html:
Metamemory and Confidence

Metamemory refers to the awareness and regulation of one’s own memory processes. It has two main components:

  • Monitoring: Judging how well one has learned or how likely a memory will be recalled (e.g., confidence judgments, “feeling of knowing”).
  • Control: Using those judgments to guide behavior (e.g., choosing what to study next, whether to answer or skip a test question).

Monitoring is linked to prefrontal cortex (especially anterior PFC / frontopolar cortex), which supports reflective evaluation of memory states. Medial parietal cortex and posterior cingulate contribute to introspective access to memory strength. Activity often dissociates from the hippocampal signal itself, showing that metamemory is not just “memory replay.”

Confidence judgments draw on lateral PFC and parietal regions that track evidence strength, partly overlapping with decision-making circuits. This can diverge from accuracy because people may be highly confident in false memories. Memory accuracy (hippocampal-medial temporal lobe) and metamemory judgments (frontoparietal network) rely on partially distinct circuits, which explains why some patients with amnesia can lose memory but still have preserved “feelings of knowing,” or conversely, why frontal damage impairs monitoring while leaving raw recall intact. In everyday life, confidence guides whether we trust a memory enough to act on it, or seek external confirmation.
